candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Hymns on the Crucifixion
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion II.5-7 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

The lamb is to be set aside on the tenth day of the month — and on this very tenth day, Ephrem reads, the true Lamb entered Jerusalem to be set aside for the slaughter. The four days between the setting-aside and the killing correspond to the Holy-Week interval between Palm Sunday and Crucifixion. Tewahedo Pascal catechesis preserves this counting in its Holy-Week observances.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Hymns on the Crucifixion
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion II.8 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

The lamb is roasted whole, eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Ephrem reads each prescription as eucharistic precedent: the unbroken lamb is the unbroken body of Christ; the unleavened bread is the bread that carries no leaven of malice; the bitter herbs are the bitter cup of the Passion. Tewahedo Anaphora retains this canonical OT prototype as one of its earliest Pascal anchors.

candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on the Crucifixion III.1-3 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

Blood struck upon the two side-posts and the upper lintel of the door traces, for Ephrem, the very figure of the Cross over each Israelite household: a mark in the shape of the salvation that the blood signifies. The destroyer who passes over the marked door does so because the mark is the Cross before the Cross. Tewahedo cites this as a canonical eucharistic-demonic-defense anchor: the Pascal blood marks the household; the eucharist marks the soul.
